title: February 7 – Alcoholic Bomb
body:
February 7 – Alcoholic Bomb

“If, when you honestly want to, you find you cannot quit entirely, or if when drinking, you have little control over the amount you take, you are probably alcoholic.”
— We Agnostics

That line right there sealed the deal for me.

Once I started drinking, I didn’t stop. And worse—I never knew when I was going to start. It could be a wedding celebration, a kid’s birthday party, or yet another breakup. A lot of the time it didn’t even need a reason. The mental obsession would kick in quietly, like a whisper I’d learned not to question, and once that first drink landed, the merry-go-round started spinning.

I couldn’t stop even when I wanted to.

It always ended the same way—drunk, remorseful, and in trouble. Again. I lived like an alcoholic bomb, just waiting to go off. No countdown timer. No warning. Just a matter of time.

If anyone drank like me, that’s a serious problem to have on your hands.

Willpower failed me big time. Every single time I said, “I got this,” it turned out I absolutely did not have it. And eventually I had to face the truth: something stronger than my own thinking was going to have to solve this problem—because my thinking was the problem.

I needed something I could work with. Something I could try to understand. Something I could make sense of enough to lean on when my own ideas ran out of gas. And it turns out, for every alcoholic, there’s a unique understanding of a Higher Power that works for them.

Thank God I uncovered one that worked for me.

What finally made you willing to entertain the idea that your way might not be the only way?

title: June 18 - Main Character
body:
We are the main character in our own lives. In fact, we're the person God has to work with. Nobody can do our praying, inventory, amends, and service work for us. That's our job.

As we grow spiritually, we start to see God show up in our lives. We react differently. We rely on prayer before disaster instead of after it. Sometimes we find ourselves thinking, Holy crap, this spiritual stuff actually worked...again.

But alcoholism is sneaky.

Sometimes spiritual growth turns into spiritual superiority. We start thinking we see something other people can't. Why aren't they doing what we're doing? Why don't they get it? If we're not careful, we can start acting like we're God's favorite, like our prayers work better than other people's, or like we've found some secret connection that everybody else somehow missed.

Let's call it what it is: arrogance.

Sure, we're the main character in our own life. But everybody else is the main character in theirs too. After all, deep down in every man, woman, and child is the fundamental idea of God. That means God isn't just working in our lives. He's working in theirs too.

The problem starts when we begin judging how God is working in other people's lives. That's where spiritual arrogance lives. We start grading somebody else's spiritual journey instead of paying attention to our own.

The moment we think we're better than someone else because we "get it," we've stepped out of humility. We've stopped being the main character in our own story and started trying to become the director of somebody else's. That's a job we retired from when we turned our will and our lives over to the care of God.

Have you ever caught yourself judging how God was working in someone else's life?

title: April 27 — No
body:
“No.” is a complete sentence.

Looking over this fourth step, we start to see that part of our problem was losing the ability to say no. Alcohol had us going along with things we didn’t feel right about, hoping it would somehow work out in our favor. And when it didn’t, we got mad, fired up the resentment machine, and went back to hurting ourselves with booze. Same cycle, over and over, getting worse as we went. By the end, we were burnt up, living like it was us versus the whole world.

Now we’re learning something simple, but powerful. We can say no.

No to things that don’t sit right. No to people-pleasing. No to putting ourselves in spots that mess with our sobriety. It might feel uncomfortable at first, but it’s a different kind of uncomfortable… the kind that actually protects us instead of hurting us.

We don’t have to explain it, defend it, or dress it up. "No." is a complete sentence.

Where in your life do you need to start saying no?
